mechanism: Chronic high-dose paracetamol (> 2 g/day for several days) potentiates the anticoagulant effect of warfarin via CYP2C9 and vitamin K cycle effects.
management: Single occasional doses are acceptable. For chronic or high-dose paracetamol, check INR within 3–5 days and adjust warfarin as needed.

mechanism: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 and displaces protein-bound warfarin, raising INR and bleeding risk. Onset is typically 2–5 days after starting.
management: Avoid the combination where possible. If unavoidable, check INR at 48–72 h and again at 5–7 days; consider an empirical 25–50% warfarin dose reduction.

mechanism: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole displaces warfarin from albumin and inhibits CYP2C9 metabolism, often causing a large INR rise within 3–7 days.
management: Choose a different antibiotic when possible. If cotrimoxazole is essential, check INR before day 5 and reduce warfarin dose proactively (commonly by 25–40%).

mechanism: Both raise serum potassium — trimethoprim by blocking the renal epithelial sodium channel and ACE inhibitors by reducing aldosterone. Hyperkalaemia and AKI risk is substantial in older or renally-impaired patients.
management: Avoid in CKD or in patients on other K+-raising drugs (spironolactone, NSAIDs). Check K+ and creatinine within 5–7 days; counsel to stop and seek review if palpitations, weakness, or syncope occur.

mechanism: NSAIDs blunt the renal prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation that ACE inhibitors rely on, raising the risk of AKI (the so-called 'triple whammy' when diuretics are added) and reducing antihypertensive efficacy.
management: Avoid chronic NSAID use in patients on enalapril, especially with diuretics or CKD. Prefer paracetamol; if an NSAID is essential, use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration with creatinine monitoring.

mechanism: Mechanism uncertain; clinical reports describe INR rise within 3–7 days of starting azithromycin. CYP3A4 inhibition is implicated.
management: Use shortest effective course; check INR at day 5–7. Counsel on bleeding warning signs.

mechanism: Fluoroquinolones (including ciprofloxacin) are associated with dysglycaemia — both hypo- and hyperglycaemia — in patients on oral hypoglycaemics, especially older adults.
management: Monitor capillary glucose during the antibiotic course; counsel the patient on hypoglycaemia symptoms. Prefer an alternative antibiotic where feasible.

references.label: FDA Drug Safety Communication: Fluoroquinolones + glucose

mechanism: NSAIDs displace warfarin from albumin (transient INR rise) AND impair platelet aggregation AND damage gastric mucosa — additive bleeding risk that exceeds the sum of the two drugs alone.
management: Avoid the combination. Prefer paracetamol for analgesia in patients on warfarin. If an NSAID is unavoidable (short course, contraindication to paracetamol), co-prescribe a PPI and check INR at 3–5 days; counsel patient on bleeding-warning signs.

mechanism: Metronidazole inhibits CYP2C9, the main metabolic pathway for the active S-warfarin enantiomer → 2-fold INR rise commonly seen within 5–7 days.
management: If a 5–10 day course is essential, pre-emptively reduce warfarin by 25–35 % and check INR at day 3 and day 7. Counsel on bleeding-warning signs.

mechanism: Rifampicin is a potent inducer of CYP2C9 / CYP3A4 / P-gp → warfarin clearance increases 2- to 3-fold within 1–2 weeks of starting and persists 2–4 weeks after stopping.
management: Anticipate the loss of effect. Check INR twice weekly during the first 4 weeks of rifampicin, increase warfarin dose proactively. After rifampicin stops, repeat INR weekly for 4 weeks and reduce warfarin back.

mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP3A4 (mainly responsible for atorvastatin clearance) and inhibits OATP1B1 (uptake) — net effect is loss of statin efficacy over weeks of co-administration.
management: Where co-administration is essential, increase atorvastatin to maximally tolerated dose (40–80 mg) OR switch to rosuvastatin / pravastatin (less CYP3A4-dependent). Re-check LDL at 8 weeks.

mechanism: Rifampicin induces UGT1A1 and CYP3A4 — halves dolutegravir trough concentrations during co-administration.
management: Double dolutegravir to 50 mg twice daily throughout rifampicin treatment AND for 2 weeks after rifampicin stops, then return to 50 mg once daily.

mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP3A4 → reduces lumefantrine AUC by ~70 % and artemether AUC by ~90 % → treatment failure / recrudescence of malaria.
management: Use IV / IM artesunate or quinine for malaria treatment in patients on rifampicin. If AL is the only option, monitor clinical response and parasitaemia daily; treatment failure should prompt a switch.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the Treatment of Malaria 2023

mechanism: Modest CYP3A4 inhibition increases atorvastatin exposure — clinically smaller than with clarithromycin / erythromycin but additive myopathy risk reported.
management: Counsel about myalgia and dark urine. Brief courses (≤ 5 days, e.g. azithromycin 5-day course for pneumonia) are usually acceptable. For longer courses, consider holding atorvastatin.

mechanism: ACE inhibitor-induced reduction in renal perfusion in volume-depleted patients can transiently raise INR by reducing warfarin clearance — usually modest.
management: Monitor INR at 1 week after ACE-i initiation or dose change. No proactive dose change required in most patients.

mechanism: Reduces gut flora that synthesise vitamin K, plus modest CYP-mediated metabolism inhibition → INR rises within 5–10 days.
management: Check INR before day 7. Reduce warfarin dose by 15–25 % at the start of doxycycline if pre-treatment INR is in the upper half of target range. Counsel on bleeding-warning signs.

mechanism: Additive CNS and respiratory depression (opioid + benzodiazepine). Black-box-warning interaction in the FDA / EMA labels.
management: Avoid where possible. If essential (e.g. palliative care, acute setting), use the lowest effective doses with continuous SpO₂ + RR monitoring; have naloxone available. Counsel about driving / alcohol.

mechanism: Ciprofloxacin is a weak CYP3A4 inhibitor; modest atorvastatin exposure increase. Stronger fluoroquinolone-tendon adverse-event risk is the bigger clinical concern.
management: Counsel about myalgia. For brief courses (5–7 days) co-administration is generally safe; for longer courses or in elderly, consider holding atorvastatin or switching antibiotic.

mechanism: Non-selective β-blockade masks adrenergic symptoms of hypoglycaemia (tremor, tachycardia) — patients lose early warning. Selective β1 blockers (e.g. atenolol, bisoprolol) have less effect but the issue persists in high doses.
management: Counsel about non-adrenergic hypoglycaemia warning signs (sweating, hunger, confusion, dysarthria) and emphasise self-monitoring. Where feasible, prefer cardioselective beta-blockers at lowest effective dose.

mechanism: Biphasic: phenytoin transiently inhibits warfarin metabolism (INR rises first 1–2 weeks) then potently induces CYP2C9 (INR falls thereafter, increasing thrombosis risk).
management: Check INR twice weekly for the first 4 weeks of any phenytoin start/stop or dose change. Anticipate dose adjustments in both directions; consider switching anticoagulant where stable.

mechanism: Phenytoin is a potent CYP3A4 + UGT1A1 inducer → lowers dolutegravir trough significantly. Risk of virological failure.
management: Avoid where possible. Use levetiracetam or sodium valproate instead, OR double dolutegravir to 50 mg twice daily. Monitor HIV viral load at 4 + 8 weeks of co-therapy.

mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP3A4 → halves praziquantel exposure with risk of schistosomiasis treatment failure.
management: If schistosomiasis treatment is necessary during TB therapy, defer praziquantel until after the rifampicin-containing intensive phase, OR use a higher praziquantel dose (60 mg/kg in 2 divided doses) under specialist supervision.

mechanism: Additive nephrotoxicity — tenofovir tubular toxicity + NSAID afferent-arteriole vasoconstriction. Risk increases in dehydration and the elderly.
management: Use paracetamol for analgesia where possible. If NSAID is essential, use the shortest course at the lowest dose and recheck eGFR + urine ACR within 1 week. Avoid in patients with eGFR < 60 on tenofovir.

mechanism: Fluconazole is a potent inhibitor of CYP2C9 — the main metabolic pathway for active S-warfarin. INR commonly doubles within 5–7 days of starting fluconazole.
management: If short course (≤ 7 days) is essential, reduce warfarin by 25–35 % on day 1 and check INR at day 3 and day 7. For chronic / high-dose fluconazole (e.g. cryptococcal consolidation phase 800 mg/day) the interaction is severe — switch to LMWH where possible.

mechanism: Moderate CYP3A4 inhibition by fluconazole increases atorvastatin exposure — additive myopathy risk especially at high statin doses or chronic high-dose fluconazole.
management: For short antifungal courses (≤ 7 days) co-administration is usually acceptable with myalgia counselling. For chronic high-dose fluconazole (e.g. cryptococcal maintenance), reduce atorvastatin to ≤ 20 mg or pause; check CK if myalgia.

mechanism: Fluconazole inhibits phenytoin metabolism (CYP2C9 / CYP2C19) — phenytoin levels rise to toxic range within 1–2 weeks.
management: Reduce phenytoin dose by 25–50 % on day 3 and check level at day 5 and day 14. Counsel toxicity warning signs (nystagmus, ataxia, confusion).

mechanism: Fluconazole inhibits CYP2C9 → reduces sulphonylurea clearance → prolonged hypoglycaemia risk.
management: Counsel patient on hypoglycaemia warning signs; check capillary glucose more frequently during course. Avoid in elderly or renal impairment.

mechanism: Omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit CYP2C19 — the enzyme that activates clopidogrel from prodrug to active metabolite. Reduces antiplatelet effect by 30–50 %; observational studies show increased recurrent ACS events.
management: Switch to pantoprazole or rabeprazole (much weaker CYP2C19 inhibition) or to an H2-blocker (ranitidine / famotidine) for gastroprotection. If omeprazole essential, separate by 12 h (clopidogrel morning, PPI evening) — partial mitigation.

references.label: FDA Drug Safety Communication: Clopidogrel + omeprazole

mechanism: Dual RAAS blockade (ACE-i + aldosterone antagonist) → hyperkalaemia risk substantially raised, especially with CKD, diabetes, or NSAID co-administration.
management: Indicated combination in HFrEF GDMT — monitor K⁺ + creatinine within 1 week, at 1 month, and 3-monthly. Stop spironolactone if K⁺ > 5.5 or creatinine rises > 30 %. Avoid in eGFR < 30.

mechanism: ARB + MRA dual RAAS blockade → hyperkalaemia, identical to ACE-i + spironolactone.
management: Indicated in HFrEF GDMT — same monitoring as ACE-i + spironolactone. Stop spironolactone if K⁺ > 5.5.

mechanism: NSAIDs blunt renal prostaglandin-mediated afferent-arteriole vasodilation that ARBs rely on. Adding a diuretic = 'triple whammy' AKI risk.
management: Avoid chronic NSAID use in ARB-treated patients. Prefer paracetamol for analgesia. If NSAID essential, use shortest course at lowest dose and check creatinine within 1 week.

mechanism: Trimethoprim blocks the renal epithelial sodium channel → hyperkalaemia, additive with ARB-induced aldosterone suppression.
management: Avoid in CKD, elderly, or those on spironolactone / K⁺ supplements. Check potassium + creatinine within 5 days.

mechanism: Additive potassium-sparing effect — trimethoprim blocks ENaC, spironolactone blocks aldosterone. Risk of life-threatening hyperkalaemia, especially in elderly + CKD.
management: Avoid combination where possible. If unavoidable, check K⁺ + creatinine within 5 days, counsel symptoms of hyperkalaemia. Stop one of the two if K⁺ > 5.5.

mechanism: Additive bleeding risk — aspirin inhibits platelet aggregation and damages gastric mucosa; warfarin lowers clotting-factor activity.
management: Avoid combination unless specifically indicated (e.g. mechanical heart valve with high CV risk). When essential, target lower INR range (e.g. 2.0–2.5) + co-prescribe PPI + close INR monitoring + bleeding-symptom counselling.

mechanism: Ibuprofen competitively binds COX-1 → blocks the irreversible acetylation aspirin would otherwise produce → reduces antiplatelet effect by ≥ 50 %. Also additive GI / renal injury.
management: Take aspirin at least 2 h before ibuprofen, OR > 8 h after. Prefer paracetamol for analgesia in patients on low-dose aspirin for cardioprotection.

references.label: FDA Safety Communication — Ibuprofen and aspirin

mechanism: Additive antiplatelet effect — usually intentional (DAPT after ACS / PCI / TIA) but adds bleeding risk.
management: Standard DAPT duration: 12 months after ACS, 1–3 months after elective PCI, 21 days after minor stroke / high-risk TIA. Co-prescribe PPI (pantoprazole — not omeprazole). Bleeding-risk score (PRECISE-DAPT).

mechanism: Non-selective β-blockade (or high-dose cardioselective) → α1-vasoconstriction is unopposed when adrenaline is given → severe hypertension + reflex bradycardia.
management: Continue adrenaline at standard anaphylaxis dose. If hypertension develops, use a vasodilator (GTN) rather than reducing adrenaline. Long-term: counsel β-blocker users to keep auto-injector and inform ED.

mechanism: Polyvalent cations (Fe²⁺) chelate dolutegravir in the gut → reduces DTG AUC by 50–80 %. Risk of virological failure.
management: Take dolutegravir at least 2 hours BEFORE or 6 hours AFTER any iron-containing supplement. Same applies to calcium / magnesium / aluminium antacids.

mechanism: Calcium chelates dolutegravir in the gut (oral co-administration) — same mechanism as iron / antacids. IV calcium gluconate during the same period as oral DTG is also clinically problematic.
management: Oral calcium-containing products → take DTG 2 h before or 6 h after. For acute IV calcium gluconate use, time DTG dose around the bolus.

mechanism: Iron chelates fluoroquinolones in the gut → 50 % reduction in ciprofloxacin absorption.
management: Take ciprofloxacin at least 2 hours before or 4 hours after iron-containing supplements. Same applies to tetracyclines, levothyroxine, mycophenolate.

mechanism: Tetracyclines chelate divalent cations (Fe²⁺) → reduced absorption of both drugs.
management: Take doxycycline at least 2 hours before or 4 hours after iron / antacids / dairy.

mechanism: Additive nephrotoxicity + ototoxicity. Loop diuretics increase aminoglycoside uptake in the inner-ear stria vascularis and can worsen hypovolaemia, magnifying tubular toxicity.
management: Avoid combination where possible. If both essential (severe sepsis with renal stress), maintain euvolaemia, daily eGFR + serum gentamicin trough, hold one drug if rising. Consider audiology baseline + at 7 days.

mechanism: Amlodipine weakly inhibits CYP3A4 → modest increase in atorvastatin exposure. Bigger concern with simvastatin (limit 20 mg/day when on amlodipine).
management: Atorvastatin doses up to 40 mg/day are acceptable; for 80 mg dose plus amlodipine consider switching to rosuvastatin / pravastatin. Counsel about myalgia.

mechanism: Both drugs are dihydrofolate-reductase pathway antagonists — additive antifolate effect → life-threatening bone-marrow suppression (pancytopenia) within 1–2 weeks, especially with weekly low-dose MTX for RA.
management: AVOID combination. If MTX patient needs antimicrobial PJP prophylaxis (e.g. on high-dose immunosuppression), switch to dapsone or atovaquone. If cotrimoxazole essential for an acute infection, hold methotrexate for the duration of antibiotic course + 1 week.

mechanism: NSAIDs compete with methotrexate for proximal tubular secretion → reduced renal clearance → toxic MTX levels with marrow suppression, hepatitis, mucositis. Greatest risk in renal impairment and high-dose MTX.
management: AVOID where possible. For RA patients on low-dose weekly MTX, occasional short-course NSAID at a low dose is usually tolerated with monitoring. For high-dose oncology MTX, suspend NSAIDs.

mechanism: Penicillins compete with MTX for renal tubular secretion → raised MTX levels and toxicity, especially at high doses.
management: Use shortest necessary antibiotic course. Counsel patient about mucositis / cytopenia symptoms. Check FBC at 1 week if both drugs are continued > 7 days.

mechanism: Iron forms an insoluble chelate with levothyroxine in the gut → absorption falls by ~50 %. Same mechanism as calcium, magnesium, aluminium.
management: Separate doses by at least 4 hours (levothyroxine first thing in the morning on empty stomach; iron at lunch / dinner). Recheck TSH 6 weeks after any change in iron co-administration.

mechanism: PPIs raise gastric pH → reduced levothyroxine dissolution and absorption (~10–20 % AUC reduction in chronic use).
management: Take levothyroxine at least 30 min before food / PPI; recheck TSH 6 weeks after starting / stopping the PPI. Increase levothyroxine dose by ~12.5 µg if TSH rises persistently.

mechanism: Tramadol inhibits serotonin reuptake and SSRIs raise synaptic serotonin → serotonin syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor, fever, autonomic instability, mental status change) within hours. Tramadol also lowers seizure threshold further with SSRIs.
management: AVOID combination where possible. Use paracetamol / NSAID / codeine for analgesia in SSRI-treated patients. If unavoidable, lowest tramadol dose, no PRN, counsel symptoms (clonus, agitation, hyperthermia) and stop both drugs if syndrome develops.

mechanism: Combined serotonergic activity — theoretical serotonin syndrome risk. Real-world incidence is low at standard doses.
management: Combination commonly used and generally safe. Counsel patient on symptoms; reassess if signs develop (tremor, clonus, agitation, hyperthermia).

references.label: AHS Consensus on serotonin syndrome + triptans

mechanism: Additive serotonergic effect + lowered seizure threshold. TCAs also impair tramadol metabolism via CYP2D6 inhibition.
management: AVOID combination where possible. Use NSAID / paracetamol or weak codeine alternatives. If essential, lowest doses and counsel seizure / serotonin syndrome signs.

mechanism: Additive serotonergic effect; SSRI inhibits CYP2D6 → raises TCA exposure, anticholinergic + cardiotoxicity.
management: Avoid routine combination. If specialist-supervised for refractory depression, start TCA at the lowest dose, monitor ECG (QT), counsel anticholinergic + serotonin symptoms.

mechanism: Clarithromycin is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor → 4–10-fold rise in atorvastatin exposure → rhabdomyolysis + AKI risk.
management: AVOID combination. Hold atorvastatin for the duration of clarithromycin (5–14 days) and resume on completion. Alternative — azithromycin (much weaker inhibitor).

references.label: FDA Drug Safety Communication: Clarithromycin + statin

mechanism: CYP3A4 + CYP2C9 inhibition → warfarin clearance falls → INR rises 2–3× within 3–7 days.
management: Reduce warfarin by 25–35 % at start of clarithromycin; check INR at day 3 and day 7. Counsel bleeding warning signs.

mechanism: Mechanism not fully elucidated — multiple case reports of INR rise within 5–10 days. Probable CYP-mediated.
management: Check INR before day 7 of tramadol. Reduce warfarin dose proactively if INR target is in upper half of range. Counsel bleeding signs.

mechanism: Additive bone-marrow suppression — hydroxyurea is myelosuppressive and cotrimoxazole adds folate-antagonist marrow toxicity. Risk of severe pancytopenia + neutropenia + opportunistic infection.
management: Reduce hydroxyurea dose by 50 % during cotrimoxazole course OR hold hydroxyurea. Check FBC weekly. Use alternative antibiotic where possible.

mechanism: Raised gastric pH reduces ferrous absorption (Fe²⁺ absorption requires acidic environment).
management: Separate by at least 4 hours (iron with vitamin C / orange juice; PPI later). Reassess at 4–6 weeks — if no Hb response, consider parenteral iron.

mechanism: Both prolong QT interval — additive risk of torsades de pointes especially with hypokalaemia / hypomagnesaemia.
management: Avoid combination where possible. If essential, baseline ECG + correct K⁺ / Mg first; monitor QTc. Single ondansetron dose ≤ 16 mg.

mechanism: NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandin-mediated lithium excretion → lithium level rises 30–60 % within 7 days; toxicity at usually-therapeutic doses.
management: Avoid combination. Use paracetamol for analgesia. If short-course NSAID essential, recheck lithium at day 3 and 7; counsel toxicity (tremor, ataxia, GI upset).

mechanism: ACE-inhibitors raise lithium level (renal mechanism) — toxicity risk especially in dehydration / elderly.
management: Avoid where possible. If ACE-i essential for HF / proteinuria, reduce lithium by 25 % and check level + creatinine at day 7.

mechanism: Thiazides cause volume depletion → reduced renal lithium clearance → 30–50 % rise in serum level.
management: Avoid combination. If thiazide essential, halve lithium dose and check level at day 3, 7, 14.

mechanism: ARBs raise lithium level by reducing renal clearance — similar mechanism to ACE-inhibitors.
management: Check lithium level at day 7 of any ARB initiation / dose change. Consider 25 % lithium dose reduction proactively.

mechanism: Carbamazepine is a potent CYP3A4 + CYP2C9 inducer → warfarin clearance doubles within 1–2 weeks; loss of anticoagulation.
management: Anticipate INR fall. Check INR twice weekly during first 4 weeks; increase warfarin dose proactively. Reverse the process on carbamazepine taper.

mechanism: Carbamazepine induces UGT1A1 → halves dolutegravir trough; risk of HIV virological failure.
management: Increase DTG to 50 mg twice daily during carbamazepine + 2 weeks after. Or switch AED to levetiracetam / lamotrigine.

mechanism: CYP3A4 induction → atorvastatin exposure falls 50–70 % → loss of LDL lowering.
management: Where co-administration essential, titrate atorvastatin to 80 mg or switch to rosuvastatin / pravastatin (less CYP3A4-dependent). Recheck LDL at 8 weeks.

mechanism: Carbamazepine induces UGT → halves lamotrigine plasma level.
management: When carbamazepine is added to lamotrigine maintenance, anticipate seizure recurrence and titrate lamotrigine up (typically double the dose). When carbamazepine stopped, taper lamotrigine to avoid toxicity.

mechanism: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase → blocks alternative azathioprine metabolic pathway → thiopurine accumulates → life-threatening bone-marrow suppression within 1–2 weeks.
management: If essential (e.g. gout in transplant recipient): reduce azathioprine to 25 % of original dose, weekly FBC. Prefer alternative urate-lowering (febuxostat) or alternative immunosuppressant (mycophenolate).

mechanism: Additive bone-marrow suppression — cotrimoxazole adds antifolate marrow toxicity to azathioprine cytopenia.
management: Avoid combination where possible. If PJP prophylaxis required, use dapsone or atovaquone instead. Acute infection: switch antibiotic; if cotrimoxazole essential, weekly FBC.

mechanism: Additive CNS + respiratory depression (FDA boxed warning 2019). Gabapentin AUC also rises ~44 % when combined with morphine.
management: Avoid combination where possible. If both essential (chronic pain), use lowest effective doses, no PRN, capnography / SpO₂ monitoring on initiation, naloxone available, opioid-overdose education to patient + carers.

mechanism: Combined serotonergic activity + tramadol metabolism reduced by CYP2D6 inhibition → serotonin syndrome + seizure risk.
management: AVOID combination. Use paracetamol / NSAID / codeine alternative. If unavoidable, lowest dose, no PRN, counsel symptoms (clonus, agitation, hyperthermia).

mechanism: SSRIs displace warfarin from albumin + inhibit CYP2C9 (fluoxetine moderate inhibitor) → INR rises within 1–2 weeks. SSRIs also increase bleeding via platelet serotonin depletion.
management: Check INR before day 7 and again at day 14 of starting fluoxetine. Anticipate dose reduction 10–20 %.

mechanism: Combined serotonergic activity — theoretical serotonin syndrome risk; real-world incidence very low.
management: Generally safe with standard doses. Counsel patient on serotonin syndrome symptoms; review combination if features emerge (clonus, autonomic instability, agitation).

references.label: AHS Position on serotonin syndrome and triptans

mechanism: Additive D2 antagonism → extrapyramidal symptoms + NMS risk + additive QT prolongation.
management: AVOID combination where possible. Use 5-HT3 antagonist (ondansetron) for nausea in patients on antipsychotic where feasible. If combination unavoidable, single dose only, counsel EPS, baseline ECG.

mechanism: Both folate antagonists → additive marrow toxicity + macrocytic anaemia.
management: Common combination in RA triple therapy; co-prescribe folic acid 5 mg weekly + FBC + LFT every 2 weeks for 3 months then 3-monthly.

mechanism: Both prolong QT — additive risk of torsades de pointes, especially with hypokalaemia / hypomagnesaemia.
management: Avoid combination where feasible. If essential, baseline ECG + electrolyte correction; single ondansetron dose ≤ 16 mg.

mechanism: Both opioid agonists + tramadol adds serotonergic effect → additive CNS depression + serotonin syndrome.
management: AVOID combination — duplicate-opioid prescribing. Pick one. Counsel patient against OTC codeine while on tramadol prescription.

mechanism: Amiodarone potently inhibits CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 → warfarin clearance falls; INR rises 2–3-fold within 1–3 weeks; persists weeks after stopping amiodarone (long t½).
management: Reduce warfarin by 30–50 % on starting amiodarone; check INR every 3–5 days for first 4 weeks then weekly until stable. Re-check after amiodarone stops; expect INR to drift down over 1–3 months.

mechanism: Amiodarone inhibits P-gp + CYP3A4 → digoxin clearance falls; levels double within 1–2 weeks. Additive bradycardia + AV-block effect.
management: Halve digoxin dose on starting amiodarone. Check digoxin level + ECG within 7 days; target serum 0.5–0.8 ng/mL.

mechanism: Amiodarone inhibits CYP3A4 + P-gp → simvastatin exposure rises 2–3× → rhabdomyolysis risk.
management: Limit simvastatin to 20 mg/day if combination essential. Switch to rosuvastatin / pravastatin (less CYP3A4-dependent). Counsel myalgia / dark urine.

mechanism: Same CYP3A4 inhibition — atorvastatin exposure rises 50–100 %. Less severe than simvastatin.
management: Use atorvastatin ≤ 20 mg/day; consider rosuvastatin / pravastatin if higher LDL targets required. Counsel myalgia.

mechanism: Both potently prolong QT — additive risk of torsades de pointes, especially with hypokalaemia / hypomagnesaemia.
management: AVOID combination. If essential, baseline ECG + correct K / Mg, continuous cardiac monitoring, lowest doses.

mechanism: Clarithromycin inhibits P-gp + CYP3A4 → digoxin levels double; reports of fatal toxicity (arrhythmia) within days.
management: AVOID where possible. If essential, halve digoxin dose, check level day 3 + 7, ECG.

mechanism: Verapamil inhibits P-gp + adds AV-node depression → 70 % rise in digoxin level + additive bradycardia / heart block.
management: Halve digoxin on starting verapamil. Check level + ECG within 7 days.

mechanism: Furosemide-induced hypokalaemia + hypomagnesaemia predisposes to digoxin toxicity (arrhythmia at therapeutic levels).
management: Maintain K > 4.0 + Mg > 0.7. Use K-sparing diuretic (spironolactone) co-therapy if appropriate (HFrEF). Recheck digoxin level + electrolytes after dose changes.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 + P-gp inhibition → apixaban exposure rises ~60 %; bleeding risk.
management: Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily during course OR use azithromycin instead. Counsel bleeding signs.

mechanism: CYP3A4 + P-gp induction → apixaban AUC falls 54 % → loss of efficacy (thromboembolic risk).
management: AVOID combination. Switch to warfarin (target INR 2.0–3.0) or LMWH for the duration of rifampicin.

mechanism: Moderate CYP3A4 + P-gp inhibition → ~20 % rise in apixaban exposure.
management: No dose adjustment usually required. Counsel bleeding signs; check Hb if symptomatic.

mechanism: CYP3A4 + P-gp inhibition raises rivaroxaban exposure ~50 %.
management: Avoid combination. Use azithromycin or non-macrolide where possible. If essential, counsel bleeding + check Hb.

mechanism: Potent CYP3A4 + P-gp induction → rivaroxaban level falls 50 % → loss of efficacy.
management: AVOID combination. Switch to warfarin or LMWH for the duration of carbamazepine.

mechanism: Common 'bridging' combination during warfarin initiation or interruption — additive bleeding risk.
management: Standard bridging practice — continue LMWH until INR therapeutic on 2 consecutive days (≥ 24 h apart). Counsel bleeding; check FBC + INR + creatinine.

mechanism: Amlodipine moderate CYP3A4 inhibition → simvastatin exposure rises ~80 % → rhabdomyolysis risk.
management: LIMIT simvastatin to 20 mg/day on amlodipine (FDA). Better to switch to atorvastatin or rosuvastatin where higher LDL reduction needed.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor — simvastatin exposure rises 10-fold → rhabdomyolysis (FDA contraindication).
management: CONTRAINDICATED. Hold simvastatin during clarithromycin course OR switch to azithromycin (much weaker CYP3A4 effect).

mechanism: Moderate CYP3A4 inhibition; simvastatin exposure rises 2–3× — myopathy risk.
management: Hold simvastatin during fluconazole course (especially > 7 days). Use rosuvastatin / pravastatin if needed.

mechanism: Verapamil CYP3A4 inhibition + OATP1B1 inhibition → atorvastatin exposure rises 50–100 %. Myopathy risk.
management: Limit atorvastatin to ≤ 20 mg/day on verapamil; counsel myalgia. Switch to rosuvastatin / pravastatin if needed at higher dose.

mechanism: Both depress AV node + reduce contractility — additive severe bradycardia / heart block / asystole. Highest risk with concurrent IV use.
management: AVOID combination especially IV verapamil + IV β-blocker. Oral combination only under specialist supervision with ECG monitoring and HR > 50.

mechanism: Fluoxetine is a strong CYP2D6 inhibitor — metoprolol exposure rises 2–5× → bradycardia, fatigue.
management: Use bisoprolol (renal/hepatic clearance, less CYP2D6) where SSRI essential, OR switch SSRI to citalopram / sertraline (weaker CYP2D6). Halve metoprolol if combination unavoidable.

mechanism: Linezolid is a REVERSIBLE non-selective monoamine oxidase inhibitor + sertraline raises synaptic serotonin → severe serotonin syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia, hyperthermia, autonomic instability) within hours.
management: AVOID combination. Stop SSRI 2 weeks before starting linezolid (5 weeks for fluoxetine — long half-life). For emergency / unavoidable concurrent use, stop SSRI immediately and monitor for serotonin syndrome ≥ 24 h. Use dapsone / aztreonam alternative where possible.

mechanism: MAOI + SSRI — severe serotonin syndrome. Fluoxetine's long half-life (active metabolite t½ 1–2 weeks) extends interaction window.
management: AVOID. Stop fluoxetine 5 WEEKS before linezolid where possible. For emergency / unavoidable concurrent use, stop fluoxetine immediately + ICU-level serotonin-syndrome monitoring.

mechanism: MAOI effect + tramadol's serotonin reuptake inhibition + active metabolite → severe serotonin syndrome + seizure threshold lowered.
management: AVOID. Use paracetamol / NSAID / weak opioid (codeine) alternative for analgesia. If unavoidable, lowest dose + ICU monitoring.

mechanism: Additive nephrotoxicity (glomerular + tubular damage) + ototoxicity (8th cranial nerve). Risk increases with prolonged use, dehydration, age > 65.
management: Avoid combination where possible. If essential (e.g. severe Gram+ + Gram- sepsis, enterococcal endocarditis), maintain euvolaemia, daily eGFR + drug-level monitoring, audiology baseline + at 7 days. Use shortest necessary course.

mechanism: Loop diuretic-induced volume depletion + electrolyte disturbance worsens vancomycin nephrotoxicity. Additive ototoxicity (stria vascularis).
management: Maintain euvolaemia + electrolyte balance. Avoid concurrent IV boluses. Audiology baseline if course expected > 7 days.

mechanism: Amphotericin causes K + Mg renal wasting → furosemide-induced hypokalaemia is additive → arrhythmia / paralysis. Both nephrotoxic.
management: Replace K + Mg pre-emptively + check daily. Use the lowest effective furosemide dose. Switch to liposomal amphotericin (less nephrotoxic). Consider spironolactone / K-supplements.

mechanism: Amphotericin-induced hypokalaemia + hypomagnesaemia predisposes to digoxin toxicity even at therapeutic levels.
management: Aggressive K + Mg replacement (target K > 4.0, Mg > 0.8). Daily digoxin level if both essential. ECG monitoring.

mechanism: Strong CYP2C9 inhibition → warfarin clearance halved; INR doubles within 5–7 days.
management: Reduce warfarin by 50 % on starting voriconazole. Check INR at day 3 + day 7. Continue close monitoring throughout antifungal course.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inhibition → atorvastatin exposure rises 3–5× → rhabdomyolysis risk.
management: Hold atorvastatin during voriconazole course. Use rosuvastatin / pravastatin if essential.

mechanism: Bidirectional: carbamazepine is a strong CYP3A4 inducer → halves voriconazole levels (treatment failure); voriconazole inhibits carbamazepine metabolism → carbamazepine toxicity.
management: AVOID combination. If essential (specialist), switch antifungal (echinocandin, amphotericin) OR switch AED (levetiracetam). Monitor both levels + toxicity if unavoidable.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor → reduces warfarin metabolism; INR rises 2-fold within 3–7 days.
management: Reduce warfarin by 25–35 % at start of erythromycin; check INR at day 3 + 7. Counsel bleeding signs.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor — simvastatin exposure rises 5–10× → rhabdomyolysis (FDA contraindication).
management: CONTRAINDICATED. Hold simvastatin during erythromycin course OR switch antibiotic (azithromycin much weaker CYP3A4 effect).

mechanism: CYP3A4 inhibition raises atorvastatin exposure 2–4× → myopathy risk.
management: Limit atorvastatin to 20 mg/day during erythromycin OR switch to azithromycin / rosuvastatin / pravastatin.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inhibition → carbamazepine exposure rises 2–3× → toxicity (ataxia, dizziness, drowsiness, nystagmus).
management: AVOID combination. Switch antibiotic (azithromycin much weaker effect). If essential, halve carbamazepine + check level at day 3.

mechanism: Both potent QT-prolongers — additive risk of torsades de pointes, especially with hypokalaemia.
management: AVOID. Use IV artesunate for severe malaria where possible. If unavoidable, baseline + 12-hourly ECG, correct K+ > 4.0 + Mg > 1.0, continuous cardiac monitoring.

mechanism: Multifactorial — quinine inhibits CYP2C9 and reduces VK-dependent factor synthesis → INR rises 2-fold.
management: Reduce warfarin by 33–50 % on starting quinine; check INR at day 3 + 5. Counsel bleeding signs.

mechanism: Additive nephrotoxicity + ototoxicity (loop diuretics increase aminoglycoside uptake in inner ear stria vascularis).
management: Avoid combination where possible. If both essential, maintain euvolaemia, daily eGFR + amikacin trough, audiology baseline + at 7 days.

mechanism: Piperacillin competes with methotrexate for renal tubular secretion → MTX accumulation → severe pancytopenia + mucositis (especially high-dose oncology MTX).
management: Hold methotrexate during piperacillin course where possible. For low-dose weekly MTX (RA), use shortest necessary antibiotic course + check FBC at 1 week.

mechanism: Additive renal-tubular toxicity (both excreted by active tubular secretion).
management: Maintain hydration (≥ 500 mL extra/day during valaciclovir). Check eGFR baseline + at 1 week. Avoid in eGFR < 60 if possible.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 + CYP2C19 induction → voriconazole AUC falls > 90 % → antifungal treatment failure.
management: AVOID combination. Use echinocandin (caspofungin / micafungin) or liposomal amphotericin B for antifungal therapy during TB treatment.

mechanism: Both potently prolong QT — additive risk of torsades, especially with methadone > 100 mg/day or hypokalaemia.
management: AVOID. If essential, baseline + monthly ECG, correct K + Mg, reduce methadone dose where feasible.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor + additive QT prolongation → methadone toxicity (sedation, respiratory depression) + torsades risk.
management: AVOID. Switch to azithromycin (weaker QT + CYP3A4) or non-macrolide. If essential, halve methadone + ECG + naloxone available.

mechanism: CYP3A4 inhibition + additive QT → methadone toxicity + torsades risk.
management: Halve methadone dose on initiation of fluconazole; baseline + day 7 ECG; counsel sedation / respiratory symptoms.

mechanism: Additive QT prolongation; torsades reported, especially with concurrent hypokalaemia.
management: Avoid combination where possible. Use cyclizine or metoclopramide for nausea. Single ondansetron dose ≤ 16 mg if essential; baseline ECG + K + Mg correction.

mechanism: Additive CNS + respiratory depression — opioid + benzodiazepine combination is the FDA / WHO highest-risk combo.
management: AVOID combination. If both essential (severe anxiety / withdrawal): lowest effective doses, daily review, naloxone available, counsel patient + family on overdose risk.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inducer → LNG-EC clearance increases → contraceptive failure.
management: AVOID. Use copper IUD (most effective EC; not metabolism-dependent), OR ulipristal acetate 30 mg, OR DOUBLE-DOSE levonorgestrel 3 mg single dose. Counsel future contraception with similar issue (use IUD or condom).

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 + P-gp inducer — same mechanism as carbamazepine.
management: AVOID. Same alternatives as carbamazepine + EC. Counsel future regular contraception — copper IUD preferred during + 4 weeks after rifampicin course.

mechanism: Potent CYP3A4 induction → ethinylestradiol AUC falls 50–80 % → contraceptive failure.
management: AVOID COC during + 4 weeks after rifampicin course. Use copper IUD / DMPA injection / progestogen-only injection.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inducer → contraceptive failure.
management: AVOID. Use copper IUD, DMPA, levonorgestrel IUD (LARC unaffected by enzyme induction). Counsel + plan during AED initiation in women of childbearing potential.

mechanism: Naltrexone is a pure µ-receptor antagonist. In opioid-dependent patient, precipitates acute severe withdrawal within minutes (sweating, agitation, vomiting, diarrhoea, tachycardia, hypertension).
management: AVOID. Confirm opioid-free for ≥ 7 days (10 days methadone) + negative naloxone challenge before naltrexone. For acute pain, use non-opioid analgesia (paracetamol + NSAID + regional). If opioid pain essential, may require 2–3× normal dose carefully — specialist input.

mechanism: Antagonises tramadol's opioid analgesic effect + precipitates withdrawal in dependent users.
management: AVOID. Use paracetamol + NSAID for analgesia. Counsel patient: opioid analgesia is essentially blocked while on naltrexone.

mechanism: Both folate antagonists + additive marrow toxicity, methaemoglobinaemia, haemolysis.
management: AVOID combination. Use ONE for PJP prophylaxis (cotrimoxazole preferred; dapsone alternative for cotrimoxazole-intolerant). If treating PJP + need dapsone-trimethoprim combo, monitor FBC + methaemoglobin closely.

mechanism: Additive antifolate marrow suppression — severe pancytopenia.
management: AVOID. Use alternative PJP prophylaxis (atovaquone) for MTX-treated patient.

mechanism: Non-selective β-blockade antagonises salmeterol bronchodilation + can precipitate severe bronchospasm.
management: AVOID. Use cardio-selective β1-blocker (atenolol, bisoprolol, metoprolol) if β-blocker essential — but caution remains in asthma. Consider non-β-blocker alternatives (CCB, ARB) in asthmatic patient.

mechanism: Additive CNS + respiratory depression at sedative doses. Useful synergy at sub-dissociative ketamine doses (opioid-sparing).
management: Common deliberate combination (ED procedural sedation, palliative care). Use sub-dissociative ketamine 0.1–0.3 mg/kg + opioid at half-dose with continuous SpO₂ / ETCO₂ monitoring + naloxone available.

mechanism: Additive GABA-A potentiation → severe CNS + respiratory depression.
management: Common deliberate combination (anaesthesia / ICU) — but ONLY with airway-trained operator + advanced monitoring. Halve dose of each when combined.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inhibition → markedly increased systemic budesonide → iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome + adrenal suppression reported.
management: AVOID combination. Switch to azithromycin (weaker effect). If short macrolide course (≤ 5 days) essential, counsel Cushing's symptoms.

references.label: EMA Drug Safety — Budesonide + Strong CYP3A4 Inhibitors

mechanism: Tiotropium + ipratropium / salbutamol-ipratropium combination is duplicate anticholinergic — additive systemic side-effects (dry mouth, urinary retention, glaucoma).
management: Use one inhaled anticholinergic only. SABA salbutamol alone in addition to tiotropium is acceptable (different receptor — β2). AVOID concurrent ipratropium + tiotropium.

mechanism: Verapamil is a P-gp inhibitor → dabigatran AUC rises 50–150 %; bleeding risk.
management: Reduce dabigatran to 110 mg twice daily (instead of 150 mg). Take dabigatran ≥ 2 h before verapamil.

mechanism: P-gp inhibition → dabigatran AUC rises 19 % (modest but bleeding signal in elderly / renal).
management: Consider 110 mg twice daily dose. Use azithromycin where alternative acceptable. Counsel bleeding signs.

mechanism: Potent P-gp inducer → dabigatran AUC falls 67 % → loss of efficacy.
management: AVOID combination. Switch anticoagulant to warfarin during rifampicin therapy.

mechanism: Modest INR rise reported (mechanism uncertain — likely displacement / CYP).
management: Check INR at week 1 + 2 of starting rosuvastatin; counsel bleeding signs.

mechanism: Octreotide suppresses insulin + glucagon + GH → alters insulin requirement (usually lower; sometimes hyperglycaemia if glucagon suppression dominates).
management: Monitor glucose 4-hourly initially; adjust insulin dose 25 % down on starting octreotide; re-monitor closely.

mechanism: Magnesium potentiates non-depolarising NMB → prolonged paralysis.
management: Reduce rocuronium dose by 25–50 % in patients on MgSO₄ for eclampsia or asthma. Train-of-four monitoring. Sugammadex for reversal.

mechanism: Aminoglycosides potentiate non-depolarising NMB at the motor end-plate.
management: Train-of-four monitoring during anaesthesia; reduce rocuronium dose 25 %; ensure full reversal.

mechanism: Mg potentiates suxamethonium block + may worsen hyperkalaemia.
management: Use cautiously in patient on MgSO₄ (eclampsia, severe asthma). Rocuronium with sugammadex preferred in this scenario.

mechanism: Both cause hyponatraemia / SIADH-like effect → severe hyponatraemia + seizures.
management: AVOID combination. Check Na+ at 24 h + 1 week if unavoidable. Fluid restriction.

mechanism: NSAIDs reduce renal water excretion → potentiated water retention + hyponatraemia.
management: Restrict fluid intake to 1 L total for 8 h after desmopressin. Monitor Na+. Use paracetamol where analgesia needed.

mechanism: Combined osmotic + loop diuresis — sometimes deliberate (cerebral oedema) but can cause severe hypovolaemia + electrolyte derangement.
management: Strict fluid balance + electrolytes every 4 h. CVP / arterial line. Replace K + Mg + Na losses.

mechanism: Additive GABA-A potentiation → enhanced sedation + respiratory depression.
management: Reduce both doses by 25–50 % when combined; have full airway management capability + naloxone-equivalent ready (no antidote for etomidate; ventilate until resolves).

mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP3A4/2B6 → efavirenz AUC falls ~25 % (less affected than other ARVs).
management: Standard efavirenz dose 600 mg OD acceptable in adults ≥ 50 kg on rifampicin TB therapy. Counsel adherence; monitor viral load at 6 months.

mechanism: Rifampicin induces UGT1A1 → dolutegravir AUC falls 54 %.
management: Add extra DTG 50 mg 12 h after TLD dose during rifampicin therapy + 2 weeks post (effectively DTG 50 mg twice daily). Resume single TLD when rifampicin stopped.

references.label: WHO HIV Guidelines 2024 — DTG with rifampicin

mechanism: Dolutegravir inhibits OCT2 → metformin AUC rises 79 %; lactic-acidosis risk + GI side-effects.
management: Cap metformin at 1000 mg/day when starting TLD. Monitor for lactic acidosis if eGFR < 60. Counsel re GI side effects.

mechanism: Rifampicin reduces lopinavir AUC ~75 % — sub-therapeutic; rifabutin preferred but rarely available in SSA.
management: Double the lopinavir/ritonavir dose to 800/200 mg BD (or super-boost with extra ritonavir 300 mg BD) during rifampicin therapy. Switch to rifabutin where available. Frequent LFTs.

mechanism: PPI raises gastric pH → atazanavir absorption drops ~75 % → virological failure.
management: AVOID PPIs with atazanavir. Switch to H2-blocker (famotidine 20 mg BD given ≥ 10 h before atazanavir) OR change ART to dolutegravir-based regimen. Antacids: separate by ≥ 2 h.

mechanism: Additive QT prolongation — both potently prolong QTcF.
management: Combination is standard in BPaL/M regimen but mandates baseline + monthly ECG (stop if QTcF > 500 ms or > 60 ms above baseline). Maintain K > 4 + Mg > 0.9.

mechanism: Additive QT prolongation in MDR-TB regimens.
management: Common deliberate combination; baseline + monthly ECG + K/Mg correction. Avoid concurrent other QT drugs (ondansetron, fluconazole, methadone).

mechanism: Amphotericin-induced renal impairment increases flucytosine levels → marrow toxicity.
management: Deliberate combination in cryptococcal meningitis induction. Daily creatinine + FBC. Adjust flucytosine for eGFR. Target trough 25–100 mg/L if TDM available.

mechanism: Mutual interaction — carbamazepine reduces valproate; valproate inhibits carbamazepine epoxide clearance → CBZ neurotoxicity.
management: Avoid combination where possible. If used, monitor CBZ + valproate levels + neuro side effects. Lamotrigine + valproate is also high-risk for rash — halve lamotrigine starting dose.

mechanism: Valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation → lamotrigine AUC doubles → severe rash / Stevens-Johnson risk.
management: Halve lamotrigine starting dose + slow titration (e.g. 25 mg alternate days for 2 weeks then 25 mg OD). Counsel re rash.

mechanism: Fluoxetine inhibits CYP2D6 → risperidone AUC rises 75 % → EPS / sedation.
management: Halve risperidone starting dose when co-prescribed with fluoxetine / paroxetine. Switch to sertraline / citalopram (weaker CYP2D6 inhibitors) where possible.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inhibition → quetiapine AUC rises 3–5× → sedation, postural drop, QT.
management: Avoid combination. Use azithromycin where alternative needed. If essential, reduce quetiapine to one-sixth of usual dose + ECG.

mechanism: Fluconazole inhibits CYP2C9 → sulfonylurea AUC rises → hypoglycaemia.
management: Counsel patient re hypoglycaemia signs; reduce gliclazide by 50 % during fluconazole course; monitor BGM TDS.

mechanism: Additive QT prolongation — piperaquine has marked QT effect.
management: Avoid combination — switch to metoclopramide / cyclizine for malaria-related nausea. If ondansetron essential, give single 4 mg dose only + ECG + correct K/Mg.

mechanism: NSAIDs displace warfarin + impair platelet function + GI mucosal injury → bleeding.
management: Avoid combination. Use paracetamol for analgesia. If NSAID essential, co-prescribe PPI + monitor INR weekly + counsel re bleeding signs.

mechanism: CYP3A4 + P-gp inhibition → loperamide CNS penetration + cardiotoxicity risk.
management: Avoid prolonged co-use. Limit loperamide to ≤ 2 days at standard dose. Switch to azithromycin if macrolide essential.

mechanism: Strong CYP2C9 induction → warfarin clearance increases → sub-therapeutic INR + thrombosis on washout overdose.
management: Avoid combination. Use DOAC where feasible. If unavoidable: monitor INR weekly during initiation/discontinuation; expect dose adjustment ~30–60 %.

mechanism: Enzyme induction → ethinylestradiol AUC falls > 50 % → contraceptive failure.
management: AVOID COC. Use copper IUD, LNG-IUD, or DMPA injection — LARC unaffected by enzyme induction.

references.label: FSRH Drug Interactions with Hormonal Contraception

mechanism: Strong CYP / UGT induction → dolutegravir + TDF metabolite clearance increases → virological failure.
management: AVOID. Switch AED to levetiracetam (no induction). If essential, double DTG to 50 mg BD + close VL monitoring at month 3 + 6.

mechanism: Sugammadex binds progestogens — equivalent to missing one COC dose. Effect lasts ~7 days due to renal excretion of complex.
management: Counsel patient: use additional barrier contraception for 7 days post-anaesthesia. Same applies for POP / implant / depot. Emergency contraception if unprotected intercourse during the 7-day window.

mechanism: Flumazenil precipitates withdrawal seizures in chronic BZD users + has shorter half-life → re-sedation when diazepam outlasts antagonist.
management: Avoid in chronic BZD users (epilepsy, panic disorder). Use ONLY for iatrogenic procedural over-sedation in benzodiazepine-naive patients. Observe ≥ 2 h post for re-sedation.

mechanism: Charcoal adsorbs ~50 % of oral NAC if given concurrently — minor effect since IV NAC is preferred for clinical poisoning.
management: If oral NAC chosen, separate charcoal + NAC by 2 h. IV NAC route avoids this entirely + is preferred for clinical paracetamol overdose.

mechanism: Additive antimuscarinic — urinary retention, tachycardia, anticholinergic delirium (esp. elderly).
management: Avoid combination in elderly + organophosphate-poisoned patients on continuous atropine. Use SABA (salbutamol) alone for bronchospasm if atropine being titrated.

mechanism: Additive sedation + seizure-threshold reduction + serotonergic effect with tramadol.
management: Avoid combination. Use ondansetron (caution QT) or metoclopramide for nausea on opioid. If essential, halve promethazine dose + monitor for sedation.

mechanism: Miltefosine is teratogenic + long half-life (7 days). Effective contraception essential through treatment + 5 months post.
management: Use copper IUD or DMPA injection during + 5 months after miltefosine — COC alone is insufficient (does NOT add to teratogenicity but ensures pregnancy avoided during high-risk window).

mechanism: Concurrent use in onchocerciasis or heavy Loa loa load → severe Mazzotti-like reaction + risk of encephalopathy.
management: Screen for Loa loa microfilaraemia BEFORE giving either drug in West/Central African endemic zones (Cameroon, Gabon, Congo). If microfilarial load > 8000/mL, hospitalise or use ivermectin-only sparingly.

mechanism: Aspirin displaces acetazolamide + acidifies blood → CNS penetration of acetazolamide → confusion, metabolic acidosis, salicylate accumulation.
management: AVOID combination. Use paracetamol for analgesia in IIH / altitude patients. If essential, reduce acetazolamide to 250 mg BD + monitor bicarbonate + salicylate.

mechanism: Systemic absorption of topical β-blocker + non-DHP CCB → severe bradycardia, AV block, hypotension reported.
management: Avoid combination. Use latanoprost (PG analogue) for glaucoma OR switch verapamil to amlodipine (DHP) for hypertension.

mechanism: Additive bone marrow suppression + peripheral neuropathy + optic neuropathy.
management: Deliberate BPaL/M combination. Linezolid dose reduction (1200 → 600 mg) if marrow / neuro toxicity. FBC + neuro + visual screen monthly.

mechanism: Additive QT prolongation.
management: Combination is occasionally used in severe MDR/XDR-TB; baseline + monthly ECG + K/Mg correction. Avoid if QTcF > 500 ms at baseline.

mechanism: Both potently prolong QT → torsades.
management: AVOID. Switch arrhythmia management to alternative (β-blocker / CCB) during VL treatment. Daily ECG if essential.

mechanism: Antibiotic clears colonic bacteria that ferment lactulose — lactulose may be less effective at lowering NH₃.
management: Lactulose + rifaximin is preferred combination for recurrent hepatic encephalopathy (rifaximin minimal absorption + adds nitrogen-fixing reduction).

mechanism: Dipyridamole inhibits cellular adenosine uptake → markedly potentiates adenosine effect → prolonged asystole.
management: Use adenosine at quarter dose (1.5 mg initial) in patients on dipyridamole. Have full resuscitation available.

mechanism: CBZ depresses AV node → additive heart block with adenosine — prolonged asystole possible.
management: Halve initial adenosine dose (3 mg) in patients on carbamazepine; have pacing capability.

mechanism: Additive QT prolongation + bradycardia.
management: AVOID. Use atovaquone-proguanil or doxycycline for chemoprophylaxis in patients on amiodarone.

mechanism: Additive QT + seizure threshold reduction.
management: AVOID. If severe malaria after mefloquine prophylaxis, use artesunate IV instead of quinine for treatment.

mechanism: Serotonin syndrome — additive 5-HT increase + lowered seizure threshold.
management: AVOID. Use paracetamol ± codeine instead of tramadol. If essential, lowest tramadol dose + counsel patient on serotonin syndrome signs.

mechanism: Additive QT prolongation + serotonergic effect.
management: AVOID combination. Use cyclizine for nausea in patients on citalopram. If ondansetron essential, ECG + single 4 mg dose.

mechanism: Serotonin syndrome via additive 5-HT effect.
management: AVOID. Use paracetamol / NSAID / codeine for analgesia. Counsel patient on serotonin syndrome.

mechanism: Treatment of hyperthyroidism reduces clotting factor catabolism → warfarin requirements fall.
management: Check INR weekly during transition to euthyroid; expect warfarin dose reduction ~25 %.

mechanism: Additive CNS + respiratory depression; pregabalin AUC rises ~40 % with morphine.
management: Reduce pregabalin starting dose to 25 mg BD when added to opioids. Counsel re overdose risk + sedation. Naloxone available.

references.label: FDA Pregabalin + Opioid Resp Depression Warning

mechanism: Methylene blue is potent MAOI → serotonin syndrome with SSRI/SNRI.
management: AVOID. Stop SSRI 5 half-lives before elective MB. In poisoning emergency (methaemoglobinaemia), give MB if MetHb > 30 % + symptomatic — outweighs serotonin syndrome risk; monitor for hyperthermia + clonus.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 induction → etonogestrel AUC falls > 80 % → contraceptive failure.
management: Implant unsuitable while on rifampicin + 4 weeks after. Use copper IUD or DMPA injection (unaffected by enzyme induction).

references.label: FSRH Drug Interactions with Hormonal Contraception

mechanism: CYP3A4 induction → contraceptive failure.
management: Use copper IUD or DMPA injection. Counsel about future LARC choice when on enzyme-inducing AEDs.

mechanism: Large doses (used in β-blocker overdose) potentiate warfarin via unclear mechanism — INR rises.
management: Monitor INR daily during glucagon infusion for β-blocker overdose; transient warfarin dose hold may be needed.

mechanism: Additive NO-mediated vasodilation → profound hypotension + reflex tachycardia.
management: Stop oral nitrate when starting nitroprusside infusion; resume after weaning off and BP stable.

mechanism: Additive negative inotropy + chronotropy → severe bradycardia + heart block + asystole.
management: AVOID combination. For rate control with β-blocker, use DHP CCB (amlodipine) for BP. Stop one if combined inadvertently — atropine + pacing ready.

mechanism: Additive bradycardia (donepezil enhances vagal tone via ACh; bisoprolol blocks sympathetic).
management: Baseline + 4-week ECG. Avoid combination in patients with sick sinus / AV block; consider memantine instead.

mechanism: Donepezil inhibits plasma cholinesterase → prolonged suxamethonium duration of action.
management: Avoid suxamethonium in patients on donepezil. Use rocuronium + sugammadex for RSI / muscle relaxation.

mechanism: Haloperidol is potent dopamine D2 antagonist → completely opposes levodopa effect → severe Parkinsonism + risk of NMS on abrupt levodopa withdrawal.
management: AVOID haloperidol in Parkinson disease. For acute agitation: low-dose quetiapine or clozapine (specialist). For nausea: domperidone (peripheral D2 only).

mechanism: Metoclopramide is D2 antagonist (central + peripheral) → opposes levodopa + worsens parkinsonism.
management: AVOID. Use domperidone for nausea in Parkinson disease (peripheral D2 only). Cyclizine acceptable.

mechanism: Additive CNS + respiratory depression — especially intrathecal baclofen.
management: Halve baclofen dose on opioid initiation; counsel re sedation; naloxone available.

mechanism: Combined hyperkalaemia + myocardial depression — reported fatal hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest during MH treatment.
management: AVOID verapamil + diltiazem during dantrolene treatment of malignant hyperthermia. Use β-blocker / amiodarone for rhythm control instead.

mechanism: Passive antibodies may neutralise live vaccine virus → reduced immune response.
management: Delay live vaccines (yellow fever, MMR, varicella, BCG) for 3 months after IM anti-D. If anti-D given within 14 days of live vaccine, revaccinate after 3 months.

mechanism: HRIG can mildly reduce active immune response to vaccine if same site / over-dosed.
management: Give HRIG into + around wound, and vaccine into deltoid (or anterolateral thigh for infants) on OPPOSITE limb. Never exceed HRIG 20 IU/kg.

mechanism: SSRIs reduce platelet aggregation + may raise INR via competitive plasma protein binding.
management: Check INR at 1 + 2 weeks after starting / stopping SSRI. Counsel re bleeding signs. Add PPI if also on NSAID.

mechanism: Additive respiratory depression — combination implicated in many overdose deaths.
management: AVOID concurrent benzodiazepine. Treat anxiety with non-pharmacological / SSRI. If both essential, lowest BZD dose + naloxone access + family counselling.

mechanism: Both antifolates — additive megaloblastic anaemia + pancytopenia.
management: AVOID combination. For toxoplasmosis + PJP co-prophylaxis: use pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin (folinic acid) → covers both. Switch to atovaquone if intolerant.

mechanism: Additive bone marrow suppression — pancytopenia.
management: Switch zidovudine to abacavir / TDF-based ART. If unavoidable, monitor FBC twice weekly + reduce ART intensity or use G-CSF.

mechanism: Additive marrow suppression.
management: Monitor FBC weekly during CMV induction; consider atovaquone for PJP prophylaxis in patients on valganciclovir.

mechanism: Severe bradycardia + heart block reported when sofosbuvir-containing regimens combined with amiodarone — mechanism unclear (autonomic / direct cardiac).
management: AVOID. If amiodarone discontinued, wait 3 months before starting DAA (amiodarone half-life). Alternative regimens for HCV + amiodarone exist (glecaprevir/pibrentasvir is also affected — refer specialist).

mechanism: Rifampicin is strong CYP3A4 + P-gp inducer → DAA AUC falls dramatically → virological failure.
management: AVOID. Defer HCV treatment until TB course complete (typically 6 months), OR use rifabutin alternative if TB regimen permits.

mechanism: TCAs block reuptake of catecholamines → potentiated pressor effect of noradrenaline → severe hypertension + arrhythmia.
management: Reduce noradrenaline starting dose 50 % in patients on TCAs / cocaine / MAOI. Continuous arterial line + cautious titration.

mechanism: Adrenaline coadministration prolongs duration + reduces systemic absorption — but adds α/β-adrenergic risks.
management: Deliberate adjunct in many regional blocks (max bupivacaine + adrenaline: 2.5 mg/kg). Avoid adrenaline-containing solutions in: end-arterial sites (digits, penis, ear, nose tip), severe coronary disease, hyperthyroidism.

mechanism: PCC provides factors II/VII/IX/X — heparin still acts on antithrombin → may cause unexpected over-anticoagulation post-reversal OR thrombosis.
management: Stop heparin infusion before PCC. If recent heparin given, consider partial protamine reversal. Restart anticoagulation as soon as bleeding controlled to reduce thrombosis risk.

mechanism: Rifampicin induction lowers atovaquone AUC ~50 % → PJP / toxo treatment failure.
management: AVOID. Use cotrimoxazole + leucovorin for PJP in patients on rifampicin (or use rifabutin instead of rifampicin if possible).

mechanism: Additive nephrotoxicity — aciclovir crystal nephropathy + NSAID-induced AKI.
management: Stop NSAID during IV aciclovir course. Use paracetamol for analgesia. Monitor creatinine daily.

mechanism: Lincosamides potentiate non-depolarising NMBs at the motor end-plate.
management: Train-of-four monitoring during anaesthesia in patients receiving clindamycin. Reduce rocuronium dose 25 %. Ensure full reversal with sugammadex.

mechanism: Fluconazole inhibits CYP3A4 → domperidone AUC rises 3× + additive QT prolongation.
management: AVOID combination. Use cyclizine or metoclopramide (NOT in Parkinson) for nausea. If essential, single domperidone dose 10 mg + ECG.

mechanism: Additive oxidative stress on erythrocytes → severe haemolysis especially in G6PD-deficient patient. Both also raise methaemoglobin.
management: Test G6PD before combining. AVOID combination in G6PD intermediate / deficient. Monitor FBC + methaemoglobin weekly.

mechanism: Additive bone marrow suppression (additive antimetabolite effect); ganciclovir + mycophenolate AUCs rise via shared renal tubular secretion.
management: Reduce mycophenolate dose by 50 % during ganciclovir course. Twice-weekly FBC. Consider switching to letermovir for CMV prophylaxis where available.

mechanism: TCA blocks noradrenaline reuptake + α1 antagonism → unpredictable hyper- or hypotensive response; usually exaggerated pressor effect.
management: Reduce phenylephrine starting dose 50 % in patients on TCA. Continuous arterial line. Avoid bolus dosing.

mechanism: Linezolid is reversible MAOI → ephedrine releases noradrenaline → severe hypertensive crisis.
management: AVOID combination. Use phenylephrine (direct-acting α agonist, less affected) instead. Stop linezolid 48 h before elective anaesthesia where ephedrine likely.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inhibition → tolvaptan AUC rises 10× → severe aquaresis + over-rapid sodium correction risk (osmotic demyelination).
management: AVOID combination. Use azithromycin for macrolide indication. Stop clarithromycin ≥ 7 days before resuming tolvaptan.

mechanism: Sevelamer binds levothyroxine in gut → absorption reduced.
management: Separate by ≥ 4 h (levothyroxine on empty stomach AM; sevelamer with meals). Recheck TSH at 6 weeks after starting / stopping sevelamer.

mechanism: Lithium enhances granulocyte release — additive leucocytosis with G-CSF; rarely problematic but watch for exaggerated response.
management: Monitor FBC twice weekly during co-administration. Reduce filgrastim dose if WBC > 50 × 10⁹/L.

mechanism: Deliberate synergy — adequate iron stores required for ESA efficacy.
management: Co-administer iron during ESA therapy. Target ferritin > 100 µg/L + TSAT > 20 %. IV iron sucrose / ferric carboxymaltose if oral iron inadequate.

mechanism: Additive oto + nephrotoxicity — loop diuretic increases aminoglycoside cochlear toxicity.
management: Avoid combination. Use indapamide / thiazide for HTN during TB injectable course. Audiometry monthly + creatinine weekly if combined.

mechanism: Fluoxetine (+ paroxetine) is strong CYP2D6 inhibitor → reduces active endoxifen metabolite of tamoxifen by 50–70 % → reduced anti-tumour effect.
management: AVOID strong CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion). Use sertraline, citalopram, escitalopram, venlafaxine for SSRI need.

mechanism: Tamoxifen inhibits CYP2C9 → warfarin metabolism reduced → INR rise + bleeding.
management: Monitor INR weekly on starting tamoxifen; expect warfarin dose reduction 25–50 %. Or switch to DOAC where appropriate.

mechanism: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2 → clozapine AUC rises 30–80 % → seizure + sedation + agranulocytosis worsening.
management: AVOID combination. Use cotrimoxazole / cephalexin / amoxicillin for UTI / RTI in clozapine patients. If quinolone essential, halve clozapine + closer monitoring.

mechanism: Recall — smoking induces CYP1A2 + reduces clozapine levels by ~50 %. Stopping smoking → clozapine levels rise + risk of toxicity (sedation, seizures).
management: When patient stops smoking (e.g. admitted to hospital + no-smoking ward), reduce clozapine dose by 25 % over 1 week + recheck plasma trough at 2 + 4 weeks. Counsel re changes.

mechanism: Additive hypoglycaemia + insulin no longer needed at full dose due to GLP-1 effect.
management: On starting GLP-1, reduce insulin by 20 % initially; check BGM 4× daily + adjust further as HbA1c improves. Patient education on hypo recognition.

mechanism: Furosemide-induced volume depletion + electrolyte loss potentiates zoledronate-induced AKI + hypocalcaemia.
management: Hold loop diuretic on day of infusion. Pre-hydrate with 500 mL saline. Ensure normocalcaemia + adequate vitamin D before infusion.

mechanism: Haloperidol is D2 antagonist → opposes cabergoline; prolactin rises again + may worsen Parkinson disease if cabergoline used for that indication.
management: Avoid combination. For psychosis with prolactinoma: switch to aripiprazole or quetiapine (less prolactin elevation). For nausea on cabergoline: use ondansetron (single dose) or cyclizine.

mechanism: Both increase synaptic monoamines + lower seizure threshold; small risk of serotonergic effects.
management: Combination acceptable for ADHD + co-morbid depression / anxiety. Start sertraline at lower dose. Watch for agitation, sweating, seizures.

mechanism: Paroxetine is strong CYP2D6 inhibitor → atomoxetine AUC rises 5× → cardiovascular + neuropsychiatric toxicity.
management: Reduce atomoxetine starting dose 50 %. Use sertraline / citalopram instead of paroxetine where SSRI needed.

mechanism: Both lower seizure threshold; bupropion increases tramadol levels via CYP2D6 inhibition.
management: AVOID combination. Use paracetamol + codeine if opioid needed. Counsel re seizure risk if combined.

mechanism: Concurrent NRT + varenicline — additive nausea + headache + adrenergic effects.
management: Combination acceptable for highly nicotine-dependent smokers (more effective than either alone per recent evidence). Counsel re increased AEs.

mechanism: Both inhibit aldehyde dehydrogenase → severe disulfiram-like reaction + psychosis reported.
management: AVOID combination. Wait 14 days after disulfiram before metronidazole. Use alternative (tinidazole has similar effect; vancomycin / clindamycin for C. difficile).

mechanism: Additive myopathy + rhabdomyolysis risk — both raise CK.
management: Consider holding statin during daptomycin course. Monitor CK weekly. Stop daptomycin if CK > 5× ULN or symptoms.

mechanism: Pyridostigmine is cholinesterase inhibitor → unpredictable NMB response in myasthenic patients (often resistant to non-depolarisers + sensitive to suxamethonium).
management: MG patients undergoing anaesthesia: use reduced rocuronium dose (one-third to one-half), train-of-four monitoring + sugammadex for reversal. Continue pyridostigmine morning of surgery.

mechanism: PPI inhibits CYP2C19 → reduced clopidogrel activation. Pantoprazole has LEAST effect of PPIs (vs omeprazole / esomeprazole).
management: Pantoprazole preferred PPI with clopidogrel where acid suppression required (or H2 blocker). Separate timing by ≥ 12 h.

mechanism: GLP-1 RAs delay gastric emptying → altered warfarin absorption + variable INR.
management: Check INR weekly during titration. Maintain consistent timing of warfarin relative to liraglutide.

mechanism: Additive fluid retention + heart failure risk; hypoglycaemia with overdosing.
management: Avoid combination in patients with HF risk. Monitor weight + signs of HF + reduce insulin on starting pioglitazone.

mechanism: Topiramate > 200 mg/day reduces ethinylestradiol AUC → contraceptive failure.
management: Use copper IUD / LNG-IUS / DMPA if on topiramate > 200 mg/day. Counsel about reduced COC efficacy + barrier method as backup if COC continued.

mechanism: Topiramate-induced metabolic acidosis additive with metformin lactic acidosis risk.
management: Check bicarbonate at baseline + 4 weeks on topiramate. Monitor for symptoms of acidosis. Stop topiramate if bicarbonate < 17.

mechanism: Anti-TNF immunosuppression + live attenuated yellow fever virus → risk of disseminated YEL-AVD.
management: AVOID live vaccines (YF, MMR, varicella, BCG, OPV) during + 6 months after biologic. Plan vaccination ≥ 4 weeks before starting biologic. Same applies for adalimumab, tocilizumab, rituximab.

mechanism: Rituximab causes HBV reactivation in HBsAg+ / anti-HBc+ patients — fulminant hepatitis reported. Deliberate combination as prophylaxis.
management: Screen HBsAg + anti-HBc before rituximab. If HBsAg+ — TDF 300 mg OD prophylaxis during + ≥ 12 months after rituximab. If anti-HBc+ only — monitor HBV DNA monthly + treat with TDF if rising.

mechanism: Additive marrow suppression.
management: Monitor FBC + neutrophils weekly during co-administration. Use atovaquone for PJP prophylaxis if marrow suppression concerning.

mechanism: Iron chelates mycophenolate in GI → reduced absorption.
management: Separate by ≥ 4 h. Recheck rejection markers / disease activity if iron started after stable on MMF.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inhibition → tacrolimus AUC rises 3–5× → AKI, neurotoxicity, hyperkalaemia, QT.
management: AVOID. Use azithromycin (weak CYP3A4 effect). If essential, reduce tacrolimus dose 50–66 % + daily trough levels + creatinine monitoring.

mechanism: CCBs (especially diltiazem) inhibit CYP3A4 → tacrolimus levels rise. Amlodipine has weaker effect than diltiazem.
management: Amlodipine preferred CCB in transplant; monitor tacrolimus trough at 1 week post initiation/discontinuation. Avoid diltiazem + verapamil.

mechanism: Additive risk of benign intracranial hypertension (BIH) — both raise CSF pressure.
management: AVOID concurrent tetracycline class (doxycycline, minocycline, lymecycline, tetracycline) during + 1 month after isotretinoin. Switch acne antibiotic to erythromycin if needed.

mechanism: Additive + synergistic cardiotoxicity — heart failure rate dramatically higher with concurrent anthracycline.
management: AVOID CONCURRENT. Sequential regimen — complete anthracycline first (e.g. AC × 4 cycles), then trastuzumab. Strict LVEF monitoring at baseline + 3-monthly. Avoid trastuzumab if LVEF falls > 10 % absolute or below 50 %.

mechanism: Aprepitant induces CYP3A4 → ethinylestradiol AUC falls → contraceptive failure during + 28 days after each cycle of aprepitant.
management: Use additional barrier contraception (or copper IUD) during + 1 month after each aprepitant cycle. Counsel patient + provide alternative.

references.label: FSRH Drug Interactions with Hormonal Contraception

mechanism: Additive nephro + ototoxicity — both irreversibly damage cochlear hair cells + renal tubules.
management: AVOID combination. Use ceftriaxone / cefepime instead of gentamicin for gram-negative cover in cisplatin patients. If unavoidable, daily creatinine + audiometry.

mechanism: Ticagrelor inhibits CYP3A4 → simvastatin AUC rises → rhabdomyolysis risk. Atorvastatin similar but less affected.
management: Limit simvastatin to 20 mg with ticagrelor (40 mg risk). Atorvastatin 40 mg + ticagrelor safe. Monitor CK if myalgia.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inhibition → ticagrelor AUC rises 7× → severe bleeding + bradycardia.
management: AVOID combination. Use azithromycin. Switch ticagrelor to clopidogrel during prolonged macrolide course if possible.

mechanism: Amiodarone inhibits CYP2D6 → flecainide AUC rises + additive pro-arrhythmic effect (CAST + class III/IC effects).
management: AVOID combination. Use one antiarrhythmic + cardiology specialist. If unavoidable, halve flecainide + continuous ECG.

mechanism: Additive QT prolongation + bradycardia + torsades.
management: AVOID combination. Class III monotherapy. Switch to one or use β-blocker + amiodarone.

mechanism: Additive respiratory depression — FDA boxed warning for all opioid + benzodiazepine combinations.
management: AVOID where possible. If concurrent for chronic pain + anxiety / spasm, lowest doses + counsel patient + family + naloxone provision.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inhibition → oxycodone AUC rises 80 % → respiratory depression.
management: Use azithromycin. If clarithromycin essential, halve oxycodone dose + monitor for sedation + respiratory depression.

mechanism: Hypotension + bradycardia + excessive sedation reported with IM olanzapine + parenteral benzodiazepine within 1 h — several fatal cases.
management: DO NOT give IM olanzapine within 1 h of parenteral benzodiazepine. Oral combinations less risk. If concurrent acute agitation, choose ONE.

mechanism: Additive QT prolongation (modest with aripiprazole).
management: Baseline + 4-week ECG. Use aripiprazole rather than higher-QT atypicals (haloperidol, ziprasidone) in cardiac patients.

mechanism: Both potent triggers of MALIGNANT HYPERTHERMIA in susceptible individuals → hypermetabolic crisis + rhabdomyolysis + hyperkalaemia + arrest.
management: AVOID in MH-susceptible patients (family/personal history). Use propofol + rocuronium + sugammadex for MH-trigger-free anaesthesia. Have dantrolene 36 vials immediately available in any OR using these agents.

mechanism: Additive myopathy + rhabdomyolysis (fibrate-statin) — gemfibrozil worst (avoid completely); fenofibrate less but still significant.
management: If statin + fibrate combination essential for mixed dyslipidaemia: use FENOFIBRATE not gemfibrozil; lower statin dose (e.g. atorvastatin 20 mg); monitor CK + symptoms. Annual review of need.

mechanism: Divalent / trivalent cations (Ca, Mg, Fe, Al) chelate INSTI → reduced absorption + viral failure.
management: Separate by ≥ 4 h. Same applies for dolutegravir, bictegravir, cabotegravir, elvitegravir. Counsel patient.

mechanism: Rifampicin strong induction of UGT1A1 + CYP3A4 → cabotegravir + rilpivirine AUC fall dramatically → virological failure + integrase resistance development.
management: CONTRAINDICATED. If TB diagnosed on injectable ART, switch to oral DTG-based regimen during + 4 weeks after rifampicin course. Severe pharmacokinetic tail risk if injectable not bridged.

mechanism: Deliberate synergistic LDL lowering — PCSK9i mechanism complements statin pathway.
management: Standard combination for FH / very high CV risk not at LDL target on max statin + ezetimibe. Additive LDL reduction ~50 % on top of statin.

mechanism: Both lower serum calcium — additive risk of severe hypocalcaemia, especially in CKD.
management: Cinacalcet often discontinued before denosumab. Check Ca + correct vitamin D before each denosumab dose. Monitor Ca weekly × 1 month after denosumab.

mechanism: Additive lowered seizure threshold + CNS stimulation + psychosis.
management: AVOID combination. Use SSRI (sertraline) for depression in Parkinson disease. If essential, lowest doses + neurological + psychiatric monitoring.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inhibition → ergot alkaloid accumulation → ergotism (severe vasospasm, ischaemia of extremities + viscera).
management: AVOID. Do not give ergometrine to a patient on a macrolide / azole. Use oxytocin ± carboprost for uterotonic need. If ergotism suspected — stop + vasodilators + specialist.

mechanism: Additive vasoconstriction (ergot + triptan) → coronary + peripheral vasospasm.
management: AVOID combination + separate by ≥ 24 h. Use alternative uterotonic (oxytocin). Counsel migraine patients postpartum.

mechanism: TCAs may blunt the IOP-lowering effect of α2-agonists + additive systemic effects.
management: Monitor IOP response; α2-agonist may be less effective. Use alternative IOP agents (timolol, acetazolamide) in acute angle closure.

mechanism: ACE inhibitors reduce renal lithium clearance → lithium toxicity.
management: Monitor lithium level closely (within 1 week) + renal function on starting/changing ACEi. Reduce lithium dose as needed.

mechanism: Additive potassium retention (MRA + ACE inhibitor) → hyperkalaemia, risk of fatal arrhythmia (especially in CKD / elderly / diabetes).
management: Monitor K + creatinine at 1 + 4 weeks + after dose change. Avoid potassium supplements + salt substitutes. Stop if K > 6.0. Deliberate combination in heart failure with close monitoring.

mechanism: Trimethoprim blocks the renal epithelial sodium channel (amiloride-like) → potassium retention; additive with ACE inhibitor → severe hyperkalaemia (esp. elderly — sudden-death signal).
management: Avoid cotrimoxazole/trimethoprim with ACEi/ARB in the elderly. Use an alternative antibiotic (e.g. nitrofurantoin for UTI). If essential, check K within 3–5 days.

mechanism: Diltiazem inhibits CYP3A4 → raised simvastatin → myopathy.
management: Limit simvastatin to 20 mg/day with diltiazem; or use a non-CYP3A4 statin (pravastatin, rosuvastatin).

mechanism: Carbapenems dramatically reduce valproate levels (rapid + profound) → loss of seizure control.
management: AVOID carbapenems in patients on valproate for epilepsy. If essential, use an alternative anticonvulsant cover + monitor levels (supplementing valproate is ineffective).

mechanism: Ceftriaxone-calcium precipitates in the lungs/kidneys of neonates — fatal precipitates reported.
management: CONTRAINDICATED in neonates (≤ 28 days) receiving IV calcium (even by different lines). In older patients, do not co-infuse via the same line; separate administration.

mechanism: SSRIs impair platelet serotonin → reduced aggregation; additive GI-bleeding risk with NSAIDs.
management: Avoid regular NSAIDs with SSRIs, especially in the elderly / peptic-ulcer history. If needed, co-prescribe a PPI + counsel re bleeding.

mechanism: Fluoroquinolone + corticosteroid → markedly increased risk of tendinopathy + tendon rupture (especially Achilles, elderly).
management: Avoid the combination where possible, especially in the elderly. Counsel to stop + rest + seek review if tendon pain occurs.

mechanism: Carbamazepine is a strong hepatic enzyme inducer (CYP3A4) that markedly lowers praziquantel plasma concentrations, risking treatment failure.
management: Avoid co-administration where possible; if praziquantel is essential (e.g. neurocysticercosis), consider higher praziquantel dosing/specialist advice and confirm parasitological cure.

mechanism: Phenytoin induces CYP3A4, substantially reducing praziquantel exposure and efficacy.
management: Avoid the combination; seek specialist advice on alternative anticonvulsant timing or praziquantel dose adjustment, and verify cure.

mechanism: Phenobarbital induces hepatic metabolism, lowering praziquantel levels and efficacy.
management: Avoid where possible; if both are required, anticipate reduced praziquantel exposure and seek specialist advice.

mechanism: Systemically absorbed ophthalmic timolol adds to verapamil's negative chronotropic/dromotropic effect, risking bradycardia and AV block.
management: Avoid or use with caution; monitor heart rate/ECG, use punctal occlusion to limit systemic timolol absorption, and prefer a non-beta-blocker IOP-lowering agent.

mechanism: Additive depression of sinoatrial/AV node conduction between systemically absorbed ophthalmic timolol and diltiazem.
management: Avoid or monitor closely (pulse/ECG); use punctal occlusion and consider an alternative anti-glaucoma agent.
